properties.snippet: To provide the public the data to see air quality trends. Moreover, the dataset provides an opportunity to see the District’s seasonal and diurnal cyclical flux of pollutants and its interaction with local weather patterns.
properties.description: This dataset contains quality assured and DOEE-certified air quality data collected from the District’s five air monitoring network sites. The dataset covers a three-year period and includes hourly concentration data points from the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)’s criteria pollutants, air toxics, and speciation. It also includes hourly surface meteorology data points. The District of Columbia is providing this data for a rolling 3-year period when data become available from the EPA. For complete history of data, visit the EPA Air Quality System API at aqs.epa.gov/aqsweb/documents/data_api.html

properties.snippet: The purpose of this dataset is to share hyper-local air quality data, consisting of PM2.5, PM10, and meteorological measurements, collected through our Purple Air network in the District of Columbia.
properties.description: This dataset is made up of hourly measurements of PM2.5 and PM10, and meteorological measurements, collected through DOEE’s Purple Air network in the District of Columbia. The meteorological data collected are the sensor’s internal temperature and relative humidity readings. Measurements are collected to gain a better understanding of hyper-local air quality data. This data is collected through 24-hour continuous measurements.

candidates.title: Report on Air Quality Trends in the District of Columbia

properties.snippet: A look back at the District's air quality from 1996 through 2025
properties.description:
To better understand the current air quality status in the District, the following summary highlights key pollutants and their compliance with the National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS). These standards are designed to ensure the air remains safe and healthy for both residents and visitors. In this context, areas are classified as either in "attainment" (meeting EPA air quality standards) or "nonattainment" (not meeting them). The summary below outlines the District's current status with respect to these classifications.

  •  Ground-Level Ozone (O3): The District and the metropolitan region are currently in moderate nonattainment status of the 2015 8-hour ground-level O3 NAAQS, though have also been determined by EPA to have attained "clean data" and are in the process of submitting a redesignation request to EPA.
  • Particulate Matter: The District is in attainment for the 2012 annual PM2.5 NAAQS and the 24-hour NAAQS. EPA strengthened the primary annual PM2.5 standard in 2024 from 12.0 μg/m³ to 9.0 μg/m³; this revised standard should be considered separately from the District's prior attainment status.
  • Carbon Monoxide (CO): The District is in attainment for the current 8-hour and the 1-hour NAAQS.
  • Sulfur Dioxide (SO2): The District is in attainment for the 2010 1-hour primary SO2 NAAQS and the 2024 annual secondary SO2 NAAQS.
  • Nitrogen Dioxide (NO2): The District is in attainment for the 2010 1-hour and the 1971 annual NAAQS.
  • Lead (Pb): The District is in attainment for the 2008 NAAQS.

candidates.title: Heritage Tree Relocations in Washington D.C.

properties.snippet: The why, when, and how of moving heritage trees.
properties.description:
Trees in the city are critical to our well-being. Among many other benefits, trees improve our air and water quality, cool our neighborhoods, and provide nurturing habitats for birds, bees, and numerous other wildlife. Large trees provide greater environmental benefits than smaller trees and are protected from unnecessary damage or removal by the Urban Forest Preservation Act and the Tree Canopy Protection Act in the District of Columbia. Any tree with a trunk greater than 100” in circumference is called a heritage tree. Heritage trees may only be removed if considered hazardous by a city arborist, otherwise, heritage trees cannot be removed, topped, girdled, or destroyed.

If a heritage tree is within the limits of disturbance of a construction project, then they need to be properly protected throughout construction. However, there are times when the site plans cannot provide adequate protection, and so the only remaining legal option is to move the tree to a safer place on the property. This is a laborious, careful process, but ultimately preserves the environmental benefits and the cultural significance of the heritage tree.

properties.snippet: E. coli monitoring data compiled in response to the January 2026 Potomac Interceptor Collapse.
properties.description:
A regional dataset containing E. coli monitoring sampling results collected along the Potomac and Anacostia Rivers, in response to the January 2026 Potomac Interceptor Collapse. Each data provider retains responsibility for its own data and submits to this compilation dataset voluntarily. Check the Source field to identify the data provider:

  • DC Department of Energy & Environment (DOEE)
  • Maryland Department of the Environment (MDE)
  • Virginia Deparment of Environmental Quality (VADEQ)
  • DC Water
  • Potomac Riverkeepers Network (PRK) with University of Maryland (UMD) 

Contact individual data providers to learn more about their data (i.e., collection, quality assurance, terms of use, etc.). Questions regarding DC Department of Energy & Environment sampling sites can be directed to pi.data@dc.gov.
